background.definition: Priapism is an abnormally prolonged and painful penile erection, typically lasting 4 or more hours, in the absence of continued sexual stimulation. Some males have recurrent attacks of priapism (“stuttering priapism”).

list.listitem: The true incidence is unknown.
Males with sickle cell disease (SCD) are more likely to experience priapism than men in the general population.
Priapism in SCD tends to occur in 2 age groups: 5 to 10 years and 20 to 25 years, although priapism is possible in all age groups.
Impotence may occur with recurrent priapism because of fibrotic changes that occur in the corpora.
Priapism is generally due to obstruction of venous outflow from the corpus cavernosa.
Injection of vasoactive drugs into the penile corpus cavernosa, including alprostadil, usually to treat erectile disorder.

Medications including phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors (PDE5is), trazodone, prazosin, chlorpromazine, and anticoagulants. Of cases of drug-related priapism submitted to the FDA, only 3% were caused by a PDE5i while 34% were caused by second-generation anti-psychotics.
Excessive sexual stimulation and activity, at least initially.
Sickle cell disease.
Penile injury or trauma.
Spinal cord injury or trauma.
Urinary tract infections, including cystitis, prostatitis, and urethritis.
Illicit drug use, including cocaine and marijuana.
Chronic myeloid leukemia and other hematologic conditions.
Pelvic vascular thrombosis.
Pelvic tumor.
Neurologic tumor.
Fat embolism.
Dehydration.
Circumcision.
Other infections, such as SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19), potentially resulting in thromboembolitic complications and/or affecting the male genital system.
Low-flow (ischemic) priapism: due to unknown or known causes, including leukemia, sickle cell, or medications. A flaccid glans penis results.
High-flow (arterial, nonischemic) priapism: due to rupture of penile artery. A rigid glans penis results.
A combination of low-flow priapism and high-flow priapism is possible.
The corpus spongiosum and glans penis are not usually directly involved in priapism.
The diagnosis is made clinically. The patient is typically a young male who presents with a painful and abnormally persistent erection. C
Distinguish ischemic from non-ischemic priapism using corporal penile blood gas and if necessary penile and peineal duplex Doppler ultrasound.C
Sickle cell disease, which is a major cause of priapism, can be diagnosed by electrophoresis. B
Priapism may occur in any age group, from newborns to the elderly. The patient is typically a young male who presents with a painful and abnormally persistent erection.
Children who present with priapism often suffer from leukemia or sickle cell disease.

The erection may have lasted more than 6 hours by the time the patient is evaluated. Urination through the erection is typically impossible, creating a distressing sense of urinary urgency. The erect penis is often darkened in color and tender to touch. Anxiety and diaphoresis may also be present.

Ischemic (low-flow) priapism is usually characterized by a fully rigid corpora cavernosa, pain, and abnormal cavernous blood gasses. Non-ischemic (high-flow) priapism typically is characterized by chronic, well tolerated tumescence without full rigidity and sometimes a history of perineal trauma.
Perform an initial diagnostic evaluation as described below:

Order a CBC with differential (including platelet count) to determine the presence of blood dyscrasias, and PT/PTT/INR (coagulation profile) to determine the presence of coagulopathies. Blood work should be interpreted in the context of the presenting symptom (priapism), as not all patients with hematologic conditions experience priapism.
Obtain a urinalysis to determine the presence of infection (eg, cystitis, prostatitis, urethritis). Culture and sensitivity is also useful for targeting a specific infectious agent.
Order urine toxicology to test for the presence of potentially causative substances and screen for psychoactive medications.
If undiagnosed sickle cell disease is clinically suspected, perform sickle cell electrophoresis to determine the presence of this disease, if suspected.
Ameriican Urologic Association (AUA) guidelines (2022) recommend corporal penile blood gas penile to distinguish ischemic (low-flow) from non-ischemic (high-flow) priapism.
Typical blood gas findings for cavernous blood with ischemic priapism include pO2 < 30 mm Hg, pCO2 > 60 mm Hg, and pH < 7.25.

If blood gas is indeterminate, perform a penile and perineal duplex Doppler ultrasound to determine the presence of ischemic (low-flow) versus non-ischemic (high-flow) priapism to determine the course of treatment.
For patients with non-ischemic priapism, consider penile Doppler ultrasound to assess the size and location of the fistula.
Determine and discontinue possible causative medications.
Determine whether priapism is nonischemic (high-flow), ischemic (low-flow), or a combination of both (eg, nonischemic that becomes ischemic) using Doppler ultrasound.
Draw blood gases from penile blood to determine the extent of possible damage. Consider nuclear scanning of the penis if tricorporal involvement is suspected.
After priapism is diagnosed clinically, urgently consult a urologist. B
Causative agents (eg, sildenafil, injection of vasoactive medications) should be discontinued immediately. B

Most cases of ischemic priapism lasting less than 36 hours can be successfully treated by aspiration and injection of alpha-adrenergic medication (phenylephrine) without the risk of causing fibrosis.C
Surgical intervention will likely be required if aspiration fails or if the priapism has lasted more than 36 hours.B
After surgical treatment return of erectile function is uncommon; consider prosthesis placement.C
Non-ischemic priapism is not an emergency and initial therapy includes a period of observation and possibly embolization if symptoms persist and treatment is desired.C
Discontinue possible causative agents (eg, sildenafil).
Most cases of ischemic (low-flow) priapism lasting less than 36 hours can be successfully treated by aspiration and injection of alpha-adrenergic medications without the risk of causing fibrosis.

An intrapenile injection involves phenylephrine, epinephrine, etilefrine, or ephedrine sulfate introduced directly into the corpus cavernosa. The agent recommended by AUA guidelines (2021) is phenylephrine because of minimal risks of cardiovascular side effects. Phenylephrine should be diluted in normal saline to a concentration of 100 to 500 mcg/mL, and 1 mL injections should be given repeatedly at 3- to 5-minute intervals for 1 hour. Monitor blood pressure and heart rate during phenylephrine therapy. If detumescence is not achieved, surgery will probably be required.
Phenylephrine is also the initial treatment option for iatrogenic priapism following intracavernosal injection for ED.
Undesirable side effects of sympathomimetics include headache, hypertension, cardiac arrhythmias, tachycardia, rebound bradycardia, and feelings of restlessness and even panic.
Oral (systemic) medications are not indicated as the sole treatment of ischemic priapism. If these agents are used, they should be administered concurrently with intrapenile injections.
The initial management of nonischemic (high-flow) priapism is conservative observation because of the possibility of spontaneous resolution.

Evidence is lacking on consistent treatments for priapism related to sickle cell disease. Three small poor quality studies compared sildanefil or stilbestrol with placebo to reduce the frequency of stuttering priapism, but found no difference between the two groups.
Stuttering (recurrent) priapism is treated like ischemic priapism, with the addition of gonadotropin-releasing hormones or antiandrogenic agents.
Introduce 12- or 16-gauge needles into the corpus cavernosa to aspirate 20 cc of blood. Arterial aspiration is only for diagnostic purposes in nonischemic priapism.
Most cases of ischemic priapism lasting more than 36 hours require one or more shunts to drain the penis and restore pelvic circulation.
Attempt multiple injections of sympathomimetics prior to surgical intervention.

AUA guidelines (2021) recommend a distal corporo-glanular shunt, with or without tunneling, in patients who have failed first-line medical therapy. In a series of 169 patients presenting with priapism, surgical intervention was more likely in those with longer duration and recurrent priapism.
If distal corporoglanular shunt fails,, consider corporal tunneling.
After surgical treatment return of erectile function is uncommon; consider prosthesis placement.
A study reported a series of six patients with good outcomes following superselective transcatheter embolization of the cavernous artery.
This is not a medical emergency and may be caused by unregulated arterial inflow associated with a fistula.
Initial management is observation for up to 4 weeks at home. Penile Doppler ultrasound can be used to assess the size and location of the fistula.,

For patients with persistent non-ischemic priapism who desire treatment, consider embolization as first-line therapy. If patients have persistent erections following embolization, repeated embolization is recommended by AUA guidelines (2021) over surgical ligation.,
Use ice packs to reduce swelling and pain.
Educate and reassure the patient and his partner.
Counsel the patient and his partner if sexual functioning has been negatively affected.
The treatment of associated conditions, such as sickle cell disease or leukemia, should be in addition to intracavernous injections in ischemic priapism.
Cold compresses, exercises, observation and oral therapies are not recommended for patients with acute ischemic priapism as they are unlikely to be successful.
Patients with sickle cell disease should be treated for ischemic priapism using intracavernous treatment along with treatment of sickle cell disease.
Patients must avoid all illicit drugs.
Patients with stuttering (recurrent) priapism may learn how to self-inject phenylephrine into the corpus cavernosa during attacks.
Aspiration of blood from the corpus cavernosa in nonischemic priapism is contraindicated.
All types of priapism are considered a urological emergency.
Priapism is probably best treated in the hospital under the supervision of a urologist.

Although not all cases of priapism require immediate medical treatment, early assessment is critical because ischemic priapism can lead to fibrosis of the corpus cavernosa with resultant loss of erectile ability.
The outlook is better if treatment is initiated early. B
Impotence is an unfortunate consequence of recurrent priapism because of the fibrotic changes that occur in the corpora. B
No proven techniques for preventing attacks of priapism have been identified. Therefore, efficient management when attacks occur is the best option at this time. B
Priapism may help identify those at risk of eventual sickle cell organ failure. C
Treatment of older patients is similar to that of younger ones, except that treatment is often more difficult and less successful in older patients.
Lower concentrations in smaller doses of phenylephrine should be used in patients with cardiovascular disease.
Leukemia and sickle cell disease are common causes of priapism in children.
Lower concentrations in smaller doses of phenylephrine should be used in children.
Gonadotropin-releasing hormones should not be administered to children due to lack of physical maturation.
